title: St Justin Martyr and the charge of subordinationism
subtitle: Order and origin in God are not inequality of nature.
summary: St Justin writes more than a century and a half before Nicaea, in words the Church had not yet fixed. He calls the Son "another God and Lord subject to the Maker of all things" and gives him "the second place". He also worships him, calls him God, and denies that the Father's essence is divided in begetting him. Everything turns on the difference between order and causal origin, what the Greek Fathers call taxis, and inferiority of nature. Drawn from the Dialogue with Trypho, the two Apologies, and Basil the Great on number and nature.
origin: Discord, dogma-exegesis: Blessed Justin Martyr is not a Subordinationist.

essay.text: A believer who reads about the Fathers online will meet the claim early and often: that the faith of Nicaea was invented in the fourth century, and that the Christians of the second century believed something else. St Justin Martyr is usually the first witness called, because he is the first Christian writer who tries at length to say how the Son stands to the Father, and because he says it in words the Church had not yet fixed. The question is not only for scholars. If the Church changed her faith once, she can change it again, and nothing she confesses is safe. So it is worth taking the hardest sentences in Justin slowly, quoting them whole, and asking what he is actually claiming.

Two very different claims travel under one word. The first is that the Son is from the Father as from his source, that the Father alone is unbegotten, and that there is an order in God, what the Greek Fathers call taxis, in which the Father is the principle and the cause. This the Orthodox Church confesses to this day and calls the monarchy of the Father. The second claim is that the Son is less than the Father in what he is, a lower grade of divinity, a being made rather than begotten. That is Arianism, and the Church condemned it. Any honest reading of Justin has to decide which of the two he is saying, and the way to decide is to let him finish his sentences.
The sentences that sound like inequality

There is no reason to hide them. In the Dialogue with Trypho, Justin undertakes to prove "that there is, and that there is said to be, another God and Lord subject to the Maker of all things." In the First Apology, presenting the faith to an emperor, he says that Christians worship Christ "having learned that He is the Son of the true God Himself, and holding Him in the second place, and the prophetic Spirit in the third." In the Second Apology he writes that "next to God, we worship and love the Word." A reader who stops there has grounds for the charge. A reader who continues finds Justin qualifying his own language within a few lines. The Son, he says, is distinct from the Maker of all things "numerically, I mean, not [distinct] in will," and has never at any time done anything the Father did not will. He is called an Angel, Justin explains more than once, not because he belongs among the angels but "because He announces to men" whatever the Father wishes announced, and "because He ministered to His will." The word is a name of office. The above and the below in these passages concern who appears in the world and who remains unseen, not who is greater.

Justin's own analogy for the begetting says more than any of his titles. When we speak a word, he says, we beget the word, "yet not by abscission, so as to lessen the word [which remains] in us"; and when one fire kindles another, the first is "not lessened when it has kindled [another], but remains the same," while the second "appears to exist by itself, not diminishing that from which it was kindled." He returns to the image near the end of the Dialogue and makes it exact: the Son was begotten "by His power and will, but not by abscission, as if the essence of the Father were divided." This is the picture the Council of Nicaea will take up when it confesses Light of Light, and Justin uses it for the same purpose, to deny that anything in God is cut, spent, or parcelled out. A man who thought the Logos a lesser being would have no reason to labour the point that the Father loses nothing. And when Justin states the relation directly, he states it as origin: the Father is "the cause of His power and of His being Lord and God." Cause is not rank. It says where the Son is from.
The Church at prayer answers first

The surest test of what a second-century Christian believed about Christ is not his vocabulary but his worship, because a Jew turned philosopher does not offer worship to a creature. Justin offers it, in public, in a document addressed to the Roman state. Father, Son, and prophetic Spirit, he writes, "we worship and adore." The Word "who is from the unbegotten and ineffable God" is worshipped and loved. The Son, "being the first-begotten Word of God, is even God." The Father alone is unbegotten and beyond naming, while the Son "alone is properly called Son." And Justin did not argue this and then walk away from it. He was put to death in Rome under the prefect Rusticus for refusing to sacrifice, and the Church numbers him among the martyrs. What a man dies confessing is the best commentary on what his sentences meant.
What Justin had not yet been given words for

None of this makes Justin a fourth-century theologian, and the Church has never needed him to be one. He has no fixed distinction between essence and person, no settled term for what the Three share and what distinguishes them, no homoousios. He arranges Father, Son, and Spirit in a sequence and leaves the sequence unexplained. In one sentence, on the most natural reading of the English, he lets the good angels stand inside a clause about worship where the Church's later language would not place them, and readers have argued over that clause ever since. These are the marks of a man working before the vocabulary existed, not the marks of a different faith. St Basil the Great, writing more than two centuries afterwards against those who wanted to number the Spirit beneath the Son, gives the rule that settles the matter: "what thing ever lost its own nature by being numbered?" Things counted remain what they were. Order in God is real, the Father is genuinely the source and the cause, and neither of those truths makes the Son or the Spirit less than God. Justin was feeling for that sentence. He did not yet have it. The Church, in her own time and through her councils, wrote it down for him, and in doing so she was not correcting his faith but naming it.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: I shall attempt to persuade you, since you have understood the Scriptures, [of the truth] of what I say, that there is, and that there is said to be, another God and Lord subject to the Maker of all things; who is also called an Angel, because He announces to men whatsoever the Maker of all things, above whom there is no other God, wishes to announce to them.
florilegium.gloss: The hardest sentence in Justin, quoted without softening. Note that in the same breath he explains what Angel means: it is a name of office, given because the Son announces the Father's will.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: He who is said to have appeared to Abraham, and to Jacob, and to Moses, and who is called God, is distinct from Him who made all things, numerically, I mean, not [distinct] in will. For I affirm that He has never at any time done anything which He who made the world, above whom there is no other God, has not wished Him both to do and to engage Himself with.
florilegium.gloss: Justin's own qualifier, a few lines later. What he is defending is a distinction of number, of who is who, not a difference of will and not a lower rank in willing.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: God begot before all creatures a Beginning, [who was] a certain rational power [proceeding] from Himself, who is called by the Holy Spirit, now the Glory of the Lord, now the Son, again Wisdom, again an Angel, then God, and then Lord and Logos; and on another occasion He calls Himself Captain, when He appeared in human form to Joshua the son of Nave (Nun). For He can be called by all those names, since He ministers to the Father's will, and since He was begotten of the Father by an act of will; just as we see happening among ourselves: for when we give out some word, we beget the word; yet not by abscission, so as to lessen the word [which remains] in us, when we give it out: and just as we see also happening in the case of a fire, which is not lessened when it has kindled [another], but remains the same; and that which has been kindled by it likewise appears to exist by itself, not diminishing that from which it was kindled.
florilegium.gloss: The analogy Nicaea will inherit as Light of Light. Its whole force is that nothing in the Father is divided, spent, or lessened by the begetting, which is a strange thing to insist upon if the Begotten were a lesser being.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: And that this power which the prophetic word calls God, as has been also amply demonstrated, and Angel, is not numbered [as different] in name only like the light of the sun but is indeed something numerically distinct, I have discussed briefly in what has gone before; when I asserted that this power was begotten from the Father, by His power and will, but not by abscission, as if the essence of the Father were divided; as all other things partitioned and divided are not the same after as before they were divided: and, for the sake of example, I took the case of fires kindled from a fire, which we see to be distinct from it, and yet that from which many can be kindled is by no means made less, but remains the same.
florilegium.gloss: Justin is fighting on two fronts at once. Against a modalist reading of the theophanies he insists the Son is really distinct. Against a ditheist reading he insists that nothing is divided: the essence of the Father is not cut.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: When Scripture says, 'The Lord rained fire from the Lord out of heaven,' the prophetic word indicates that there were two in number: One upon the earth, who, it says, descended to behold the cry of Sodom; Another in heaven, who also is Lord of the Lord on earth, as He is Father and God; the cause of His power and of His being Lord and God.
florilegium.gloss: The whole question in one clause. The Father is the cause of the Son's being Lord and God. Cause is not superiority of nature, it is origin, and the Church confesses it still: from the Father, the one principle, the Son is begotten and the Spirit proceeds.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: Therefore neither Abraham, nor Isaac, nor Jacob, nor any other man, saw the Father and ineffable Lord of all, and also of Christ, but [saw] Him who was according to His will His Son, being God, and the Angel because He ministered to His will; whom also it pleased Him to be born man by the Virgin; who also was fire when He conversed with Moses from the bush.
florilegium.gloss: Angel is explained again, and the explanation is a work, not a rank of being: because He ministered to His will. The above and below in Justin concern who is seen and who is not.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: For if you had understood what has been written by the prophets, you would not have denied that He was God, Son of the only, unbegotten, unutterable God.
florilegium.gloss: The plain confession. The Son is God, and the Father alone is unbegotten. Unbegottenness is the Father's personal property, not a higher grade of divinity.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: Our teacher of these things is Jesus Christ, who also was born for this purpose, and was crucified under Pontius Pilate, procurator of Judæa, in the times of Tiberius Cæsar; and that we reasonably worship Him, having learned that He is the Son of the true God Himself, and holding Him in the second place, and the prophetic Spirit in the third, we will prove.
florilegium.gloss: The text most often produced as proof of subordinationism, quoted whole. Note what it actually says alongside the second place: the Son of the true God himself, and worship offered to him.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: But both Him, and the Son (who came forth from Him and taught us these things, and the host of the other good angels who follow and are made like to Him), and the prophetic Spirit, we worship and adore, knowing them in reason and truth, and declaring without grudging to every one who wishes to learn, as we have been taught.
florilegium.gloss: The confession of Christian worship: Father, Son, and prophetic Spirit. The clause about the good angels is one of the genuinely difficult sentences in Justin, and the parenthesis around it is the translators' punctuation rather than Justin's. What the sentence as a whole shows is the Church at prayer, not a ladder of gods.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: For they who affirm that the Son is the Father, are proved neither to have become acquainted with the Father, nor to know that the Father of the universe has a Son; who also, being the first-begotten Word of God, is even God.
florilegium.gloss: Written to a Roman emperor, in public: the Word is God. Justin's argument in this chapter is against collapsing the Son into the Father, not against confessing his divinity.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: But to the Father of all, who is unbegotten, there is no name given. For by whatever name He be called, He has as His elder the person who gives Him the name. But these words, Father, and God, and Creator, and Lord, and Master, are not names, but appellations derived from His good deeds and functions. And His Son, who alone is properly called Son, the Word, who also was with Him and was begotten before the works, when at first He created and arranged all things by Him, is called Christ, in reference to His being anointed and God's ordering all things through Him.
florilegium.gloss: The Son alone is properly Son. Justin's Father is the unbegotten and unnameable source, which is exactly what later Orthodoxy will call the monarchy of the Father.

florilegium.author: St Justin Martyr
florilegium.text: For next to God, we worship and love the Word who is from the unbegotten and ineffable God, since also He became man for our sakes, that becoming a partaker of our sufferings, He might also bring us healing.
florilegium.gloss: Another sentence critics quote and then stop. Justin worships the Word. A Jew turned philosopher does not offer worship to a creature, whatever else he is prepared to say.

florilegium.author: St Basil the Great
florilegium.reference: Chapter XVII, §43, NPNF Second Series, vol. 8
florilegium.text: Nay, without exception, what thing ever lost its own nature by being numbered? Is it not the fact that things when numbered remain what they naturally and originally were, while number is adopted among us as a sign indicative of the plurality of subjects?
florilegium.gloss: Two centuries later Basil states the rule that settles the question. Number is a sign of how many, not a measure of what. Order within the Trinity is real and it does not make the Son or the Spirit less God.

scripture.note: The Lord appears to Abraham at the oak of Mamre, the theophany Justin argues over for a dozen chapters of the Dialogue.
The Lord rained fire from the Lord out of heaven, Justin's central proof that Scripture itself names two.
The Angel of the Lord in the bush who then says I AM. Justin reads him as the Son, so that Angel here means messenger, not creature.
Wisdom brought forth before the works, quoted by Justin for the begetting before all creatures and later turned by the Arians to the opposite purpose.
The Word was with God and the Word was God. The distinction and the divinity stand in one verse.
My Father is greater than I, read by the Fathers of the Son's origin from the Father and of his assumed humanity, never of a lesser divinity.
